name: AI Incident Management and Reporting
question: When an AI system causes harm, who decides, who is told, and by when?
summary: Operational incident response restores service; AI incident management is the governance around it. It defines what counts as an AI incident (unfair decisions, harmful or false outputs, privacy leaks, unsafe actions, security compromise, not just outages), sets a severity scale, keeps a register with owners and evidence, and runs notification playbooks with the clocks that may apply: for example CERT-In’s 6-hour reporting of cyber incidents, DPDP breach intimation to the Data Protection Board and affected people, sector regulators such as RBI, SEBI or IRDAI, and serious-incident reporting under the EU AI Act for high-risk systems. Each incident ends with a root cause, corrective actions and a report to the board or risk committee, and the register feeds risk reviews. This is an educational summary, not legal advice; confirm current obligations with counsel. On-call response and trace replay are covered by Incident Response in module 11.
useCases: Regulated firms using AI in credit, claims, trading or customer service
Any AI system that makes or shapes decisions about people
Organisations adopting ISO/IEC 42001 or the NIST AI RMF

S1–S4 by people affected, harm, reversibility and regulatory exposure

Keep one register with owners, evidence and a timeline for every incident
Build notification playbooks with clocks and pre-approved templates per regulator
Close with root cause and verified corrective actions; review themes quarterly
pitfalls: Treating a biased model as “working fine” because nothing crashed
Discovering the notification clock after it has run out
Closing incidents on a fix that was never verified, so they recur
tools: An incident register (Jira, ServiceNow or a GRC tool)
remember: Define it, grade it, log it, notify on the clock, fix the cause.

steps.title: Define what counts
steps.text: Arogya Kosh, a fictional health insurer, agrees with risk, legal and compliance which harms count as AI incidents and how to grade them from S1 to S4. Unfair outcomes and privacy leaks count, not just outages.

steps.title: Register and grade
steps.text: Every signal that may be an AI incident opens a register entry with an owner, the traces as evidence and a severity.

steps.title: Start the clocks
steps.text: The playbook lists which notifications may apply, with deadlines from the detection time and pre-approved templates. A privacy leak starts the DPDP breach steps; a cyber attack the CERT-In 6-hour report; claims decisions may need a note to IRDAI.

steps.title: Fix the cause, then close
steps.text: An incident closes only with a root cause and corrective actions whose fix passes the regression cases added for it.

steps.title: Report and learn
steps.text: Closed incidents go to the quarterly risk committee pack with themes and repeat rates.

steps.title: Two real-looking cases
steps.text: A claims triage model rejected 1,240 valid claims from one region (S2, decisions reversed); the chatbot showed 38 customers another person’s policy number (S2, DPDP breach steps).

pros: Harms that never crash a service are still caught
Deadlines are met because the clocks are known in advance
One register gives regulators and auditors a clear record
Repeat incidents fall when fixes must be verified
cons: Needs agreement across risk, legal, compliance and engineering
Definitions need updating as systems change
Over-reporting fatigue if severity is poorly calibrated
avoidWhen: Leaving AI harms to the IT outage process alone
Waiting for a first incident to decide who must be notified

practice.scenario: Arogya Kosh, a fictional health insurer, found that its claims triage model had rejected 1,240 valid claims from one region, and that its chatbot had shown 38 customers another person’s policy number. Neither caused an outage, so the IT process ignored them for days. It now has a written AI-incident definition with an S1–S4 scale, one register with owners and evidence, and a playbook listing the notifications that may apply (the DPDP breach steps, CERT-In for cyber incidents, IRDAI for claims decisions) with deadlines and pre-approved templates. Incidents are classified in about 2 hours, notifications go out on time, and repeats fall from 9 a year to 2. This is an educational example, not legal advice.

practice.analogy: A hospital’s adverse-event reporting system: not only when the lights go out, but whenever a patient could have been harmed, with a form, a severity grade, a deadline and a follow-up review.

library.name: pydantic
library.what: A typed incident record makes the register consistent and easy to export for audits.

practice.note: The notification rules listed are illustrative examples; which apply, and their exact deadlines, must be confirmed with legal and compliance for your sector and the current rules.

samples.code:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from pydantic import BaseModel

CLOCKS = {                       # illustrative; confirm with legal and compliance
    "cyber_incident": ("CERT-In report", timedelta(hours=6)),
    "personal_data_breach": ("DPDP: detailed report to the Board", timedelta(hours=72)),
}

class AIIncident(BaseModel):
    title: str
    system: str
    harm: str                    # unfair, false, privacy, unsafe, security
    severity: str                # S1..S4
    detected_at: datetime
    owner: str
    triggers: list[str] = []

    def deadlines(self):
        return {CLOCKS[t][0]: self.detected_at + CLOCKS[t][1] for t in self.triggers if t in CLOCKS}

inc = AIIncident(title="Chatbot showed another customer's policy number", system="support-bot",
                 harm="privacy", severity="S2", detected_at=datetime(2026, 9, 14, 10, 30),
                 owner="risk-oncall", triggers=["personal_data_breach"])
print(inc.deadlines())

numericDrill.question: A privacy breach is detected at 10:30 on Monday. If a detailed report is due within 72 hours, by what time on which day is it due? Give the number of hours after Monday 00:00.
numericDrill.answer: 10.5 + 72 = 82.5 hours after Monday 00:00, which is Thursday at 10:30.

interview.question: How is AI incident management different from IT incident response?
interview.answer: IT response restores service. AI incident management also covers harms that never cause an outage, such as unfair decisions, false or harmful outputs and privacy leaks, and adds a definition, severity scale, register, notification clocks, root cause and verified corrective action, and reporting to the risk committee and regulators.

interview.question: What would you put in an AI incident playbook?
interview.answer: Harm types and severity criteria, owners, which notifications may apply with deadlines and templates, evidence to capture, and closure criteria. Confirm the rules with legal and compliance.

mistakes.fix: Define harms such as unfair outcomes and privacy leaks as incidents
Require root cause and a verified corrective action
